edits.english: A dilemma was raised before them [it was asked of them, the students]: If the court issued a ruling that forbidden fat is permitted, and a minority of the congregation performed the transgression on its basis, and that court died and another court stood in its place, and again issued the same ruling to permit, and a different minority performed the transgression, what will be the *halakha*?

And they elaborate: According to the opinion of the one who says that the court alone brings the offering, do not raise the dilemma [do not ask, do not be in doubt] for yourself — as those judges who ruled and on whose basis the majority of the congregation acted are not here, for the first court has already died. Rather, when you should raise the question for yourself — it is according to the opinion of the one who says that the congregation is the one that brings the offering. If so, what [is the *halakha*]? And the sides of the question are: The congregation exists [stands], for together it is found that a majority of the congregation sinned.

edits.hebrew: אלא כי תיבעי לך כו' - צריך עיון: האם היה אפשר לשאול גם לשיטת מאן דאמר בית דין מייתי אם מתו מיעוט ציבור הראשונים ולא נודע כי אם אל אלו החיים, האם אומרים בית דין [חייבים] דמכל מקום הם הורו שלא כדת או לא? והא דנקט מת בית דין ולא נקט הורו בית דין אחר, דלא אפשר כי אם בסנהדרי גדולה:
או לא בעינן ההוא בית דין דהורו להם מעיקרא דתהוי להו ידיעה - כלומר, לא בעינן דתהוי להו ידיעה לבית דין קמא ומצטרפי:

edits.english: Or perhaps [maybe] we require [we need] the awareness of that court that issued the ruling; and that court no longer exists! This question was not resolved and remained as a *teiku* [it shall stand] in its place.

There is room to say that only when the court that issued the ruling itself later retracted and decided that it had erred — then the public brings an offering. But the decision of another court would not have this law, rather the congregation would be considered as if they acted due to the error of individuals.
